title: IB Music Progress Review Prep for Fall
summary: Prepare for your fall IB Music progress review by organizing evidence, explaining musical decisions, handling critique, and planning practical next steps.
body_markdown:
A fall IB Music progress review is usually a **school-designed checkpoint** , not a separate assessment required by the IB. Your teacher may examine portfolio evidence, hear unfinished work, confirm authenticity, and identify priorities before later coursework deadlines.


Effective **IB Music progress review prep** means showing what you explored, what you attempted, how your work changed, and what you will do next. A polished performance alone rarely demonstrates the full development process.


### Understand what the review is checking


The current IB Music course is organized around three musical processes: **exploring** , **experimenting** , and **presenting** . At HL, students also complete **The contemporary music maker** , a collaborative project based on real-life music-making practices.


The[official IB Music course overview](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/the-arts/music/) describes students working as researchers, creators, and performers. A useful review should therefore examine development across these roles, not only the quality of a finished recording.


Component SL weighting HL weighting Main evidence


Exploring music in context 30% 20% Written exploration and practical exercises


Experimenting with music 30% 20% Report with creating and performing experiments


Presenting music 40% 30% Finished created and performed works with programme notes


The contemporary music maker Not applicable 30% Multimedia documentation of a collaborative project


These are official course components, but your school determines the fall review's date, duration, format, and grading status. Ask whether it is formative, whether it affects a school grade, and which components you must present.


### Build a compact review portfolio


Create an organized folder or presentation rather than bringing every file without explanation. Include:


- A one-page overview of current work
- Selected composition drafts, scores, DAW exports, or improvisations
- Rehearsal recordings and concise practice notes
- Listening analysis, research sources, and citations
- Reflections showing decisions and revisions
- Unfinished tasks and current musical problems
- HL collaborative project evidence, where relevant


Use consistent filenames such as` Experiment_Creating_AOI2_V2` or` Performance_Rehearsal_2026-09-18` . Clear organization makes development traceable and leaves more review time for musical discussion. RevisionDojo's guide to[structuring an IB Music portfolio](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-structure-your-ib-music-portfolio) provides a practical organizational model.


### Select evidence that demonstrates development


Include evidence from different stages. For one composition, you might show an initial sketch, a revised score, and a current audio export.


Annotate each item using five prompts:


- **Intention:** What were you trying to achieve?
- **Action:** Which musical technique did you use?
- **Evidence:** Where can it be heard or seen?
- **Evaluation:** What succeeded or remained weak?
- **Next step:** What will you change?


Avoid vague claims such as, “I improved the texture.” A stronger explanation is: “At 0:48, I replaced sustained keyboard chords with imitative clarinet and violin entries. The contrapuntal idea became clearer, although the lower register remains crowded.” Timestamps, bar numbers, and named musical features turn opinion into evidence.


Use the[IB Music portfolio checklist](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-to-include-in-an-ib-music-portfolio) to identify missing drafts, recordings, or reflections.


### Prepare to explain musical decisions


Your teacher may ask why you changed an interpretation, selected a production technique, or connected material to an area of inquiry. Practise explaining decisions aloud using this sequence:


1. State the musical decision.
2. Identify the research, stimulus, or listening evidence behind it.
3. Explain the intended effect.
4. Evaluate the result honestly.
5. Propose a realistic revision.


For example: “I replaced block chords with a syncopated ostinato to create forward motion. It improved continuity, but it competes with the melody in bars 25-32, so I will simplify the bass rhythm there.”


Strong reflection is analytical rather than autobiographical. The guide to[writing IB Music reflections](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-write-reflections-in-your-ib-music-portfolio) explains how to connect evidence, impact, and revision.


### Check each musical process


### Exploring


Connect **musical features to context** . Naming syncopation, modal harmony, heterophony, or electronic processing is insufficient unless you explain how the feature functions and why it matters in its setting. Record credible sources and avoid unsupported cultural generalizations. See the guide to[connecting analysis with cultural context](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-connect-musical-analysis-to-cultural-context) .


### Experimenting


Experiments should show purposeful testing rather than simply unfinished work. Identify the variable changed, such as harmony, instrumentation, tempo, articulation, texture, or production, and compare the outcomes. Keep unsuccessful attempts when you can explain what they revealed and how they informed the next version.


### Presenting


For performing, review accuracy, phrasing, stylistic awareness, articulation, coordination, sound quality, and expressive intention. For creating, examine structural coherence, control of musical elements, notation or production clarity, and communication of your intention.


Programme notes should refer to audible details, influences, structure, and important revision choices. The[IB Music programme-notes guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-write-program-notes-for-ib-music-compositions) provides further examples.


### The contemporary music maker at HL


Bring evidence of planning, collaboration, your individual role, musical decision-making, and evaluation. Document rehearsals, role changes, technical choices, and responses to collaborators rather than relying only on the final product. Follow school consent and safeguarding procedures when recording other people.


### Follow a 7-day preparation plan


Time Main task Result


7 days before Confirm format and required components Expectations are clear


6 days before Audit recordings, scores, and journals Missing evidence is identified


5 days before Select and label representative drafts Development becomes visible


4 days before Make a current recording or export Present ability is documented


3 days before Revise analytical reflections Claims are supported


2 days before Rehearse a 3-minute explanation Spoken reasoning becomes concise


1 day before Test files, links, citations, and backups Technical problems are minimized


Review day Listen, take notes, and ask questions Feedback becomes actionable


Do not spend the final evening redesigning slides while neglecting the music. Clear organization matters, but musical evidence and reflection matter more.


### Turn critique into an action plan


Separate feedback into **musical** , **documentary** , and **technical** categories. Musical comments might concern phrasing or harmonic direction; documentary comments might identify weak evaluation; technical comments might involve clipping, notation, citations, or inaccessible files.


Ask focused questions:


- Where am I describing rather than evaluating?
- Is my evidence sufficient to demonstrate experimentation?
- Which revision would make the greatest difference?
- What must remain entirely my own work?


Convert each priority into a dated, observable task. Replace “improve performance” with “record bars 41-64 at three tempos and compare rhythmic stability by Friday.” Feedback does not permit another person or an AI tool to compose, perform, or rewrite assessed work for you. Keep drafts and version histories to support authentication, and check the guide to[common IB Music coursework pitfalls](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-pitfalls-that-lower-marks-in-ib-music-coursework) .


### Conclusion


A successful fall review presents **organized evidence, informed decisions, honest evaluation, and achievable next steps** . Confirm your school's requirements, show work from several stages, and connect every important claim to audible or notated evidence.


RevisionDojo's[IB Music syllabus breakdown](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-music-syllabus-breakdown-what-students-need-to-know) , Study Notes, Jojo AI, Coursework Review, and Tutors can help clarify terminology and test your reflection. Use them for guidance while keeping the musical judgment and submitted work authentically your own.
